musical.title: Company
musical.setting: New York City — various apartments and locations
musical.vocal_style: Sondheim — complex harmonies, intricate rhythms, word-painting, conversational to soaring. Demands musicianship.
musical.synopsis: Bobby (or Bobbie in the 2018 gender-swapped revival) is single, turning 35, and surrounded by five married couples who love, exasperate, and worry about them. Through a series of vignettes exploring each couple's relationship, Bobby confronts the fundamental question: is being alive the same as really living? A groundbreaking concept musical about love, marriage, and the terror of commitment.
musical.notes: The 2018 Marianne Elliott revival gender-swapped Bobby to Bobbie (female) with some couples also adjusted. Both versions are commonly produced. This data covers the original version with notes on the revival where relevant.

roles.name: Robert (Bobby) / Bobbie (revival)
roles.description: A charming, attractive, perpetually single person turning 35 who is the connecting thread between five married couples. Bobby is everyone's best friend but nobody's partner. Witty, evasive, terrified of commitment, and slowly realizing that being safe is not the same as being alive. The entire show is filtered through Bobby's perspective.

vocal.style_notes: Sondheim demands precise pitch, rhythm, and diction. 'Being Alive' is one of the great musical theatre climaxes — must build from conversational to devastating power. Must handle complex rhythms and harmonies. Emotional truth in every note.

dance.notes: Not a dance role. Physical presence and staging. Must be present and reactive even when not singing.

acting.emotional_range: extreme — charm, evasion, wit, loneliness, fear, breakthrough, vulnerability
acting.notes: One of the most demanding acting roles in musical theatre. Bobby is onstage almost constantly, often reacting rather than acting. Must convey the inner journey through a character who spends most of the show hiding their feelings. The breakthrough in 'Being Alive' must feel earned by everything that came before.

casting_insights.why: One of Sondheim's greatest roles. Demands extraordinary acting, vocal musicianship, and emotional depth. 'Being Alive' is a career-defining moment. This role elevates performers permanently.
casting_insights.common_casting: Charismatic, attractive performer with genuine Sondheim chops and deep emotional access. Must be someone you'd want as your best friend — and someone who makes you worry about them.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: 'Being Alive' is one of the 5 greatest moments in musical theatre. Nail it, and you'll never be forgotten.

recommended_for: serious musical theatre performers ready for their biggest challenge
singers with strong musicianship wanting dramatic depth
actors who can carry a show through presence

common_mistakes: playing Bobby as sad from the start
tips: Bobby's superpower is charm. Everyone loves Bobby because Bobby never lets anyone close enough to hurt them. That's not sadness — it's strategy. Play the charm genuinely, and let the cracks show slowly. By 'Being Alive', the walls should come down completely.

key_songs.title: Company
key_songs.notes: Opening. Bobby's friends calling. The cacophony of love surrounding them. Complex ensemble piece.

key_songs.title: Someone Is Waiting
key_songs.notes: Bobby imagines the ideal partner (composed of all friends' qualities). Beautiful, tentative, revealing.

key_songs.title: Marry Me a Little
key_songs.notes: Bobby wants commitment... but on their terms. Conditional love. Heartbreaking in its limitations.

key_songs.title: Being Alive
key_songs.notes: THE climax. Bobby breaks through fear into genuine desire for connection. One of the greatest songs ever written. Must be devastating.

key_songs.title: Barcelona
key_songs.notes: Morning-after scene. Comedic, sexy, evasive. Bobby trying not to commit.

roles.name: Joanne
roles.description: The sharpest, most cynical, most truthful of the wives. She's on her third marriage, drinks too much, and sees through everyone's pretense — especially Bobby's. She sings 'The Ladies Who Lunch' — one of the greatest songs in musical theatre. She's terrifying because she tells the truth.

vocal.style_notes: Powerful, sardonic belt. 'Ladies Who Lunch' is a volcanic eruption of bitterness and truth. Needs a voice that can cut glass. Think Elaine Stritch — conversational to explosive.

acting.emotional_range: high — wit, bitterness, vulnerability beneath acid, truth-telling, seduction, self-loathing
acting.notes: Must be simultaneously terrifying and sympathetic. Joanne says the things nobody else will. Her proposition to Bobby at the end is a pivotal moment — it can be played many ways but must be charged. She's the character who forces Bobby's breakthrough.

casting_insights.why: 'The Ladies Who Lunch' stops the show cold. It's one of the 10 most famous songs in musical theatre. This is a role that makes reputations. Joanne dominates every scene she's in.
casting_insights.common_casting: Formidable actress-singer with razor wit and a voice that could strip paint. Often the most experienced performer in the cast.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: 'Ladies Who Lunch' is a career-making song. One performance can define a career. Elaine Stritch, Patti LuPone — this role creates legends.

recommended_for: powerful belters wanting a defining role
performers ready to own the stage

common_mistakes: trying to be Elaine Stritch instead of finding your own Joanne
not enough vocal power for the song
tips: Joanne is the most honest person in the room and it's killing her. She drinks because she sees too clearly. She's not mean — she's heartbroken by the gap between what love promises and what it delivers. Find THAT, and 'Ladies Who Lunch' becomes nuclear.

key_songs.title: The Ladies Who Lunch
key_songs.notes: THE showstopper. Joanne eviscerates her social class and herself. Builds from sardonic observation to primal scream. Must stop the show.

key_songs.title: The Little Things You Do Together
key_songs.notes: Sardonic commentary on marriage. Joanne's wit shines.

key_songs.title: Company (finale)
key_songs.notes: Part of the ensemble supporting Bobby's journey.

roles.name: Sarah
roles.description: One half of the most physical couple — she and Harry are always either fighting or exercising. Sarah is competitive, intense about food/diet, and a karate expert. Their scenes are among the funniest in the show.

vocal.style_notes: Strong ensemble voice. Must handle Sondheim's complex harmonies and rhythms. Character voice with energy.

dance.notes: Karate/physical combat scene with Harry is a highlight. Physical comedy more than dance.

acting.notes: Physical comedy essential. The karate scene must be hilarious and slightly unhinged. Must show genuine love underneath the competition.

casting_insights.why: Fun featured role with a great comedy scene. Good Sondheim introduction without the pressure of a solo. The karate scene is memorable.
casting_insights.common_casting: Physical actress with comedy chops and musical ability.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: The karate scene gets huge laughs. A committed Sarah makes it a highlight.

tips: Sarah MUST win. At everything. Always. It's not aggression — it's how she shows love. She and Harry are perfect for each other because they're both insane in the same way.

key_songs.title: The Little Things You Do Together
Side by Side by Side / What Would We Do Without You
key_songs.notes: Major ensemble number. Couples celebrate Bobby.

roles.name: Harry
roles.description: Sarah's husband — equally competitive, slightly less intense. Their relationship is defined by constant one-upmanship disguised as love. The recovering-from-something aspect adds depth beneath the comedy.

vocal.style_notes: Sondheim ensemble. Must be precise and musical. Character delivery.

dance.notes: Physical combat scene with Sarah. Physical comedy focus.

acting.notes: Foil to Sarah. Must play the straight man to her intensity while being equally competitive.

casting_insights.why: Solid supporting role in a Sondheim show. Good introduction to the material without heavy vocal demands.
casting_insights.common_casting: Physical actor with comic timing and musical ability.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: The couple's scenes are comedy gold when both performers commit fully.

tips: Harry loves Sarah AND is terrified of Sarah. That combination is the comedy. He's as competitive as she is — he's just learned to hide it better.

key_songs.title: The Little Things You Do Together

roles.name: Amy (or Jamie in revival)
roles.description: Half of the about-to-be-married couple (with Paul/Jamie). Amy is having a full breakdown on her wedding day, singing 'Getting Married Today' — one of the most virtuosic patter songs in musical theatre. She's panicking, hilarious, and deeply relatable to anyone who's ever been terrified of commitment.

vocal.style_notes: 'Getting Married Today' is one of the hardest songs in the canon — rapid-fire patter at breakneck speed with perfect diction, building to hysteria. Must be rhythmically precise while appearing to fall apart. Extraordinary vocal control required.

dance.notes: No dance. Physical comedy and frantic staging in 'Getting Married Today'.

acting.emotional_range: extreme — panic, hysteria, love, fear, humor, eventual peace
acting.notes: 'Getting Married Today' is a masterclass in controlled hysteria. Must appear to be completely falling apart while executing incredibly precise vocal technique. The comedy must be real — she's genuinely terrified.

casting_insights.why: 'Getting Married Today' is one of the most talked-about moments in any Company production. It's a viral-worthy performance when done well. Incredible showcase for technical vocal ability and comedic acting.
casting_insights.common_casting: Technically gifted singer-actress who can handle the patter AND the comedy. Must be sympathetic even in full meltdown mode.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: 'Getting Married Today' makes careers. If you can sing it, everyone in the audience will know your name.

recommended_for: technically gifted singers wanting a defining moment

what_directors_look_for: can they actually sing 'Getting Married Today'? (non-negotiable)
tips: Amy loves Paul. She wants to marry Paul. She just happens to be absolutely terrified of marriage. The comedy comes from the gap between how she FEELS (love) and how she's BEHAVING (total meltdown). Practice the patter until it's in your bones — then forget technique and play the panic.

key_songs.title: Getting Married Today
key_songs.notes: One of the hardest songs in musical theatre. Rapid patter over a hymn. Hysteria, humor, genius. THE Amy showcase.

roles.name: Paul (or Jamie in revival)
roles.description: Amy's patient, loving fiancé/husband. He's calm, steady, and the perfect counterbalance to Amy's hysteria. Minimal singing but an important grounding presence.

vocal.style_notes: Ensemble vocals. Minimal solo demands. Must be solid Sondheim ensemble singer.

acting.emotional_range: moderate — patience, love, quiet concern, steadiness
acting.notes: The straight man to Amy's panic. Must convey genuine love and patience. Often the most grounded person in the room.

casting_insights.why: Small but important role. Great introduction to Sondheim without heavy demands. Good for building stage confidence.
casting_insights.common_casting: Warm, grounded actor who can be a calm center.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: Paul's quiet presence makes Amy's scenes work. A good Paul is essential even if not flashy.

recommended_for: actors who excel at supporting work

common_mistakes: not enough investment in limited scenes
tips: Paul loves Amy enough to wait through a meltdown. That patience isn't passive — it's the most active form of love in the show.

roles.name: Peter
roles.description: Susan's husband — the couple who are getting divorced but seem happier than anyone. Their scenes explore the irony that ending a marriage can sometimes be the most loving thing to do.

vocal.style_notes: Sondheim ensemble. Precise, musical, character-driven delivery.

acting.notes: The comedy of being happier divorced than married must land without being cruel. Genuine warmth with Susan.

casting_insights.why: Supporting role in a Sondheim classic. Good experience, manageable demands.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: The divorcing couple scenes are poignant and funny. Good material to work with.

tips: Peter and Susan are genuinely happier apart. That's not sad — it's liberating. Play the joy of a good divorce.

key_songs.title: Sorry-Grateful
key_songs.notes: Husbands reflect on marriage. One of Sondheim's most beautiful ensemble pieces.

roles.name: Susan
roles.description: Peter's wife/ex-wife. Sophisticated, content, part of the ironic divorcing couple. In the revival, this character was merged with others.

acting.emotional_range: moderate — contentment, irony, genuine care, independence
acting.notes: Similar to Peter — must sell the happy divorce concept with warmth and humor.

casting_insights.why: Solid supporting role in a Sondheim classic.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: The divorce scenes offer sharp comedy and genuine insight.

tips: Susan chose freedom and she's thriving. Show that without smugness.

roles.name: Jenny
roles.description: David's wife — the pot-smoking couple who are trying too hard to be cool. Their scene where they share marijuana with Bobby is a comedy highlight. Jenny is nervous, eager to please, and slightly manic.

vocal.style_notes: Sondheim ensemble. Character voice with nervous energy.

dance.notes: No dance. Physical comedy in the marijuana scene.

acting.emotional_range: moderate — nervousness, eagerness, comedy, genuine warmth
acting.notes: The marijuana scene is all about comic timing. Must play the desperation to be seen as cool while being deeply uncool.

casting_insights.why: Fun supporting role with a great comedy scene. Low pressure Sondheim introduction.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: The marijuana scene gets big laughs. A great Jenny makes it a highlight.

common_mistakes: not enough commitment to the bit
tips: Jenny wants Bobby to think she's cool. She's not cool. She's a suburban wife who bought pot for the first time. That gap is everything.

roles.name: David
roles.description: Jenny's husband. The other half of the pot-smoking couple. Slightly more relaxed than Jenny but equally uncool in his attempts to be hip.

acting.notes: Supports Jenny's energy. Complicit in the pot scene comedy.

casting_insights.why: Small role in a great show. Good Sondheim introduction.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: Solid supporting work that builds ensemble experience.

recommended_for: performers wanting any Sondheim stage time

tips: David goes along with Jenny's plans because he loves her. Simple as that.

roles.name: Marta
roles.description: One of Bobby's three girlfriends. Marta is a passionate, free-spirited New Yorker who loves the city with fierce intensity. She sings 'Another Hundred People' — a brilliant, complex Sondheim number about urban loneliness and connection.

vocal.style_notes: 'Another Hundred People' is rhythmically complex, lyrically dense, and emotionally layered. Must handle Sondheim's intricate rhythms while conveying genuine passion for the city.

acting.notes: Must embody New York energy. Passionate, intelligent, slightly overwhelming.

casting_insights.why: 'Another Hundred People' is a Sondheim masterpiece and a great solo showcase. Small role, big song. Perfect for building Sondheim credentials.
casting_insights.common_casting: Powerful mezzo-belt with intelligence and intensity.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: 'Another Hundred People' is unforgettable when performed well. It's the hidden gem song of Company.

common_mistakes: not connecting emotionally to the lyrics
tips: Marta loves New York the way some people love a person — completely, irrationally, and with open eyes. 'Another Hundred People' is a love letter to a city that doesn't love you back. Sing it like you mean every word.

key_songs.title: Another Hundred People
key_songs.notes: Sondheim masterpiece about NYC. Complex rhythms, dense lyrics, builds beautifully.

roles.name: April
roles.description: Another of Bobby's girlfriends — a slightly ditzy flight attendant. Her 'Barcelona' scene/duet with Bobby is a comedy highlight about the morning after and the desperate attempt to avoid real connection.

vocal.style_notes: Must handle 'Barcelona' duet — conversational, funny, sexy. Character singing quality.

acting.notes: 'Barcelona' requires impeccable comic timing in a very intimate scene. Must be funny without being cruel to the character.

casting_insights.why: Fun small role with one great scene. 'Barcelona' is memorable and fun to perform.
casting_insights.common_casting: Attractive, funny singer-actress with good comic timing.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: 'Barcelona' is a comic gem. A great April makes it a highlight.

recommended_for: performers wanting Sondheim experience in a manageable role

tips: April isn't stupid — she's just not thinking about the same things Bobby is. She had a nice time and is going to work. Bobby's the one making it complicated.

key_songs.title: Barcelona
key_songs.notes: Morning-after comedy duet with Bobby. Sexy, funny, evasive.

roles.name: Kathy
roles.description: The third girlfriend — the one who could have been 'the one.' She's smart, warm, and genuinely cares about Bobby. She's the missed opportunity that haunts the show.

vocal.style_notes: Ensemble vocals. Featured in some numbers. Sweet, genuine vocal quality.

acting.notes: Must convey genuine connection with Bobby that he's too afraid to pursue. The missed-opportunity poignancy is essential.

casting_insights.why: Small but emotionally important role. Good Sondheim introduction.
casting_insights.common_casting: Warm, genuine actress who makes you believe she could have been Bobby's person.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: If the audience feels the missed connection, Kathy has done her job beautifully.

tips: Kathy is the real thing and Bobby knows it. She's the person who makes 'Being Alive' necessary.

roles.name: Larry
roles.description: Joanne's third husband. Patient, wealthy, slightly defeated. He's learned to navigate Joanne's barbs with quiet grace. Their dynamic reveals volumes about marriage as negotiation.

acting.emotional_range: moderate — patience, quiet love, resignation, dignity
acting.notes: Must convey that he stays with Joanne by choice, not weakness. His patience is a form of love.

casting_insights.why: Quiet supporting role opposite the showiest character. Good for performers who excel at understatement.
casting_insights.common_casting: Distinguished, patient actor with quiet presence.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: Being the calm in Joanne's storm is its own art form.

tips: Larry chose to marry Joanne THREE times. He knows exactly who she is and loves her anyway. That's not weakness — it's the strongest love in the show.

key_songs.title: Sorry-Grateful
key_songs.notes: Husbands reflecting. Larry's perspective is uniquely earned.
